messages.subject_clean: Beginner's question on latent Gaussian field and Gaussian approximation to its full conditional
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA people,

I am currently starting to look into INLA for using it on models for pathogen dispersal in plant ecology.
I would first like to thank the creators and maintainers of the R-INLA site for their great work!

After working through several INLA papers, I now have a rather theoretical question about the construction of the latent gaussian vector x and the gaussian approximation of pi(x|y,theta), using the Rue, Martino, Chopin 2009 (RMC in the following) notations.
I have a small toy example (which, of course, is not necessarily a „good“ model in practice) that I want to implement by myself and which should be useful to explain the points that I do not understand or that I possibly misunderstand.
Here's the model:

eta = mu + z
mu normal variable with precision tau_mu
z  a normal random vector (of length 100, for instance) with diagonal precision matrix with entries tau_z
mu and z are assumed to be independent
y_i Poisson distributed according to exp(eta_i)

I could think of two possible parametrizations of x: either x=(eta,mu) or x=(z,mu)
Following RMC Section 2.2, we want the conditional distribution of y_i to depend only on one single x_i, so we should use the x=(eta,mu) parametrization (?). Otherwise, y_i would depend on z_i and mu, leading to complications in the Newton-Raphson algorithm used to get the Gaussian approximation and leading to a non-sparse precision matrix  in the approximation due to dependence of y_i on z_i and mu (?).
Now with Cov(mu, eta_i) = Cov(mu,mu) = tau_mu^{-1}, we get a sparse covariance matrix for x,
with nonzero entries on the diagonal and in the last row and the last column.
However, the precision matrix would then not be sparse, contrary to what is desired for applying INLA.
How could this problem be avoided?
In the mode x*(theta) of the full conditional pi(x|y,theta), what do we take for mu*? There is no observation y_i directly associated to mu, so I am not sure how it has to be treated. Would it be necessary or useful to impose some linear constraints on x? (like mean(eta_i)=mu ?)

Thanks for your comments and elucidation on these questions.

Best,

Thomas

messages.body_plain:
On 08/01/15 10:47, Thomas Opitz wrote:
> I could think of two possible parametrizations of x: either x=(eta,mu)
> or x=(z,mu)

Like Håvard just replied, R+INLA uses a third option, but it's worth
saying a few more words on this topic.  In the model you describe, the
(eta, mu) parameterisation would actually be just fine, and would not
generate dense precisions; it's the _covariance_ that becomes dense.

eta_i = mu + z_i
Prec(mu) = tau_mu
Prec(z) = tau_z I, number of z_i:s is n_z
y_i ~ Po(exp(eta_i))

The joint precision for eta and mu is a block matrix
   [tau_z I,    -tau_z 1;
    -tau_z 1^T, tau_mu + n_z tau_z]
(since the _conditional_ precision for eta given mu is the same as the
_marginal_ precision for the z-vector)

In the Newton optimisation, the contribution from the data likelihood
(via the second order derivatives) only affects the diagonal (only the
upper left diagonal block), and the precision sparsity stays sparse.

In addition, using the (z, mu) parameterisation would _also_ be ok for
this stage!  In this model, the latent model precision would be
   [tau_z I, 0;
    0, tau_mu]
and the observation model y_i ~ Po(exp(mu + z_i)) would affect the
diagonal, but also the final row and the final column.
(d^2 / dz_i dz_j of the log-likelihood is zero when i \neq j, so they
don't contribute).
The resulting sparsity will therefore be the same as in the (eta, mu)
parameterisation, and the Newton step would work in exactly the same
way as there.

It's the later steps of the INLA method that really needs the "may use
only one element of eta" restriction.  The Newton step is fine as long
as the sparsity structure of the observation dependence on eta is
similar to that of the latent model itself, and this is why the
extended representation shown by Håvard is used in the general
implementation, even though in this special case, (eta, mu) would
have also fulfilled the restriction.

Finn

I'm trying to using INLA to fit a joint model of longitudinal and survival models. Those two models are connected by sharing some same fixed effect and random effects, for example,

The longitudinal model is:
Y_ij = Xi'beta + Hij'delta + Ui'Zij,
where i stands for subject and j stands for jth measure within ith subject and  Xi = (Xi1, Xi2)and Hij =(Hi1, Hi2*tj) are fixed effects, Ui is the subject specific random effects (two dimensional) and Zij = c(1, tj),

> On 08/01/15 10:47, Thomas Opitz wrote:
> > I could think of two possible parametrizations of x: either x=(eta,mu)
> > or x=(z,mu)
>
> Like Håvard just replied, R+INLA uses a third option, but it's worth
> saying a few more words on this topic.  In the model you describe, the
> (eta, mu) parameterisation would actually be just fine, and would not
> generate dense precisions; it's the _covariance_ that becomes dense.
>
> eta_i = mu + z_i
> Prec(mu) = tau_mu
> Prec(z) = tau_z I, number of z_i:s is n_z
> y_i ~ Po(exp(eta_i))
>
> The joint precision for eta and mu is a block matrix
>    [tau_z I,    -tau_z 1;
>     -tau_z 1^T, tau_mu + n_z tau_z]
> (since the _conditional_ precision for eta given mu is the same as the
> _marginal_ precision for the z-vector)
>
> In the Newton optimisation, the contribution from the data likelihood
> (via the second order derivatives) only affects the diagonal (only the
> upper left diagonal block), and the precision sparsity stays sparse.
>
> In addition, using the (z, mu) parameterisation would _also_ be ok for
> this stage!  In this model, the latent model precision would be
>    [tau_z I, 0;
>     0, tau_mu]
> and the observation model y_i ~ Po(exp(mu + z_i)) would affect the
> diagonal, but also the final row and the final column.
> (d^2 / dz_i dz_j of the log-likelihood is zero when i \neq j, so they
> don't contribute).
> The resulting sparsity will therefore be the same as in the (eta, mu)
> parameterisation, and the Newton step would work in exactly the same
> way as there.
>
> It's the later steps of the INLA method that really needs the "may use
> only one element of eta" restriction.  The Newton step is fine as long
> as the sparsity structure of the observation dependence on eta is
> similar to that of the latent model itself, and this is why the
> extended representation shown by Håvard is used in the general
> implementation, even though in this special case, (eta, mu) would
> have also fulfilled the restriction.
>

i'm currently investigating how to use INLA approach to fit a DLM with a trigonometric 2-harmonics seasonal component.

So far i've been using the 'dlm' package, but i'm assessing how to switch to INLA approach for later more flexibility (e.g. apply a censored model).

In a first step, i'm trying to fit a DLM with INLA with the similar model as i've been using with 'dlm', that is: a 2 order polynomial component + a trigonometry 2-harmonics seasonal component (supposing that 2 cycles are likely to occur by year)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am continuing to work on the multinomial likelihood with INLA.  I am trying to extend to a case where each of the categories in the multinomial has a unique underlying random field, but cannot figure out how to build in the spde model using 'replicate' or 'copy'.  I think I am having trouble with the indexing of the multiple spdes, as i get an error message:

Note: method with signature ‘TsparseMatrix#Matrix#missing#replValue’ chosen for function ‘[<-’,
 target signature ‘dgTMatrix#ngCMatrix#missing#numeric’.
 "Matrix#nsparseMatrix#missing#replValue" would also be valid
Error in inla(formula.spde, family = "poisson", data = inla.stack.data(st.est),
f(i). Covariate does not match 'values' 1491 times. Indexes for mismatch:2470 2471, (list of indexes follows).

I am wondering whether:
1) I have correctly set up the simulation of 3 spde fields as spatial random effects for the Multinomial.
2) the building of the spdes and A matrices in the model are correct
3) how to correctly call for multiple spdes at the same points so that they will properly contribute to the Multinomial likelihood.

Simulation code is attached and pasted below.

Many thanks in advance,

Tom Bird

##############################################

### MNP with SPDE

### T Bird Dec 2014

### This borrows code from: http://people.bath.ac.uk/fl353/isba/isbaspde.R

### and http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-I-have-multinomial-data-but-I-cannot-find-the-multinomial-likelihood-isn-t-it-available-

## First, define the SPDE and generate the GRF

require(INLA)

require(lattice)

n = 1000

m=3

points = matrix(runif(n*2),n,2)

##############  Triangulation mesh

mesh = inla.mesh.create.helper(

  points=points,

  cutoff=0.05,

  offset=c(0.1,0.4),

  max.edge=c(0.05,0.5) )

## Plot the mesh and the data locations

plot(mesh)

points(points[,1],points[,2],pch=20,col="red")

##############  A matrix

A=inla.spde.make.A(mesh,

  loc=points,

  index=rep(1:n,times=m),

  repl=rep(1:m,each=n) )

##############  Make 3 spdes

## parameters for the 3 spde's

sigma0 = c(3,1,0.25)   ## Standard deviation

range0 = c(2,1,0.2) ## Spatial range

## Convert into tau and kappa:

kappa0 = sqrt(8)/range0

tau0 = 1/(sqrt(4*pi)*kappa0*sigma0)

## Construct spde objects for each class and set priors

## that will be used by inla().

spde1=inla.spde2.matern(mesh,

  B.tau=cbind(log(tau0[1]),1,0),

  B.kappa=cbind(log(kappa0[1]),0,1),

  theta.prior.mean=c(0,0),

  theta.prior.prec=c(0.1,1))

spde2=inla.spde2.matern(mesh,

  B.tau=cbind(log(tau0[2]),1,0),

  B.kappa=cbind(log(kappa0[2]),0,1),

  theta.prior.mean=c(0,0),

  theta.prior.prec=c(0.1,1))

spde3=inla.spde2.matern(mesh,

  B.tau=cbind(log(tau0[3]),1,0),

  B.kappa=cbind(log(kappa0[3]),0,1),

  theta.prior.mean=c(0,0),

  theta.prior.prec=c(0.1,1))

# make mesh index with 3 replicates for the 3 spdes

mesh.index=inla.spde.make.index(name="field",n.spde=spde1$n.spde, n.repl=3)

## set precision for spdes

Q1=inla.spde2.precision(spde1,theta=c(0,0))

Q2=inla.spde2.precision(spde2,theta=c(0,0))

Q3=inla.spde2.precision(spde3,theta=c(0,0))

## Sample from spdes

x1=as.vector(inla.qsample(n=1,Q1))

x2=as.vector(inla.qsample(n=1,Q2))

x3=as.vector(inla.qsample(n=1,Q3))

#x123=cbind(as.vector(A %*% x1),as.vector(A %*% x2),as.vector(A %*% x3))

x123=cbind(as.vector(A %*% c(x1, x2, x3)))

x123mat=matrix(x123, n,m)

## project sampled spdes onto lattice for visualization

proj1 = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1), dims=c(200,200))

proj2 = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1), dims=c(200,200))

proj3 = inla.mesh.projector(mesh, xlim=c(0,1),ylim=c(0,1), dims=c(200,200))

### Show spde fields

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

image(inla.mesh.project(proj1,field=x1))

image(inla.mesh.project(proj2,field=x2))

image(inla.mesh.project(proj3,field=x3))

################################

#  generate the data

#  2 datasets: y2 has no spde

#  y has spde for each level

################################

size = 5  # size of multinomial draw

sum.to.zero = TRUE  #  constraint for betas centered on 0

y2= y = x = idx = jdx = c()

## regression coefs

beta = rnorm(m)

## sum to zero?  set mean of coefs to 0

if (sum.to.zero)

beta = beta - mean(beta)

for(i in 1:n) {

   xx = rnorm(m, sd = 1) ## covariate values

   # Linear terms, with and without random field

   # x123 mat is the realization of the random field from above

   eta = beta * xx + x123mat[i,]

   eta2= beta * xx

   x = c(x, xx)

   ## index for location (Intercept)

   idx = c(idx, rep(i, m))

   ## index for group (beta)

   jdx = c(jdx, 1:m)

   p = exp(eta)

   p2=exp(eta2)

   prob = p/sum(p)

   prob2= p2/sum(p2)

   yy = rmultinom(1, size = size, prob = prob)

   y = c(y, yy)

   yy2 = rmultinom(1, size = size, prob = prob2)

   y2 = c(y2, yy2)

}

## dummy covariates for each field

b1=(jdx==1)*x

b2=(jdx==2)*x

b3=(jdx==3)*x

################################

#  Run some models

################################

###########  Run models with spde

## stack the data with the spde

st.est=inla.stack(

  data=list(y=y),

  A=list(A,1),

  effects=list(

    c(mesh.index, list(offset=1)),

     list(data.frame(idx=idx, jdx=jdx,

          i=idx,j=jdx,

       i1=idx, #ifelse(jdx==1, idx, NA),

       i2=idx+n, #ifelse(jdx==2, idx, NA),

       i3=idx+2*n, #ifelse(jdx==3, idx, NA),

       b1=b1, b2=b2, b3=b3))),

   tag="est")

### No spde, covariates as linear terms with dummy variables

formula.no.spde = y ~ -1 +

   ## one intercept pr multinom observation

   f(idx, model="iid",

    hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(0.000001),fixed = TRUE))) +

    f(jdx,  model="iid",

        constr = sum.to.zero,

        hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(0.001),fixed = TRUE))) +

b1+b2+b3

formula.spde = y ~ -1 +

   f(idx, model="iid",

    hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(0.000001), fixed = TRUE))) +

   f(jdx,  model="iid",

        constr = sum.to.zero,

        hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(0.001),fixed = TRUE))) +

   ## none of these parameterizations works:

   #1. using 'copy' # f(i1, model=spde1) + f(i2, copy="i1") + f(i3, copy="i1") +

   #2. using 'replicate'# f(i, model=spde1, replicate = "j")

   #3. independent fields # f(i1, model=spde1)+   f(i2, model=spde2)+   f(i3, model=spde3)

   f(i, model=spde1) + b1 + b2 + b3 # this works if mesh$n > n, but it is wrong

r.no.spde = inla(formula.no.spde,

        family = "poisson",

        data = data.frame(y2, idx, jdx, b1, b2, b3),

control.predictor= list(compute=TRUE),

        control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

### This gives me an error unless n < spde$n.spde

r.spde = inla(formula.spde,

        family = "poisson",

        data = inla.stack.data(st.est),

        ## need this for the prediction

  control.predictor= list(A=inla.stack.A(st.est),compute=TRUE),

  control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

## compare to truth (only when mesh$n > n)

betas.spde=(cbind(est.no.spde = r.no.spde$summary.fixed[,1],

  est.spde = r.spde$summary.fixed[,1],

  truth = beta))

print(apply(betas.spde,2, FUN=function(x) exp(x)/sum(exp(x))))

###########################

### predictions are for later...

Here an example:

# generic0 example from http://www.r-inla.org/models/latent-models

n=100

rankdef=1, constr=TRUE, diagonal=1e-05)
result1 = inla(formula1, data=data, family="gaussian")

Q <- Qr

but for me this behaviour is different than for other parameters.

Thanks for your support!

On 18/01/15 10:29, Marcial Marín wrote:
>      Let f(s) the spatial effect included in my model; then

The default _prior_ for kappa depends on the mesh, yes.  Q is based on
basis functions on the mesh, so inherently depends on the mesh.

> Both tau and kappa are
> linear combinations of a set of theta;

log(tau) and log(kappa), yes.  Not tau and kappa themselves.

> the set of theta follows a
> multivariate normal distribution

Yes.

> and that would be the reason why f(s)
> is multivariate normal too.

No, f(s) _conditionally_ on tau and kappa (i.e. on theta) is
multivariate Gaussian regardless of what prior is put on theta.

> We define prior distribution on theta set.

Yes.

> Is this correct?

Partly yes, partly no, as detailed above.

> I fso, which prior would be defined by default in INLA?
> log Gamma(0, 5e-5) for any theta, as is for other parameters? N(0,0.1)?

As per previous email, inla.spe2.matern by default attempts to set a
sensible prior median for the spatial correlation range, by choosing
the prior mean of the theta vector.  The user needs to help by
specifying a sensible prior median for the variance, via
prior.variance.nominal.  The _precision_ for theta is by default 0.1,
which means that the standard deviation of each theta component is
approximately 3.  Note that this is in the _log_ scale for tau and
kappa, so it's related to the _relative_ deviation from the prior median.

Finn
